Environmental Impact Assessment: Summary of Findings

The proposed extension of the gravel quarry on the eastern side of the valley has been studied for fourteen months. The consultants sampled groundwater at nine boreholes, counted traffic on the access road at four locations, and interviewed forty-two residents of the three nearest hamlets. The county council commissioned the work after an earlier application was refused because the noise modelling had been inadequate.

Groundwater. The aquifer beneath the eastern meadow feeds seven private wells. Readings taken in spring and autumn show that the water table falls by about a metre in dry years but recovers within two seasons. Dewatering during extraction would, the consultants say, lower it by at most half a metre, and only close to the pit.

Traffic. The access road carries about eleven hundred vehicles a day, one in twenty of them heavy goods vehicles. The applicant proposes sixty extra lorry movements per working day. Because the road passes a primary school and two sharp bends, the report recommends a routing agreement and a wheel-washing facility.

Ecology. The hedgerows along the northern boundary are ancient and support several locally rare species. The buffer strip proposed by the applicant would reduce, but not remove, the risk of disturbance in the nesting season. Work near the hedgerow should be restricted to the months between September and February.

Noise and dust. Night-time background noise in the hamlets is about thirty-five decibels. Modelling suggests extraction would raise it by three decibels at the nearest dwellings, which most people would barely notice. Dust is harder to predict, so continuous monitoring at the site boundary is recommended for the first two years.

The extent to which these mitigations would actually be enforced is, in the consultants' view, the central question. Planning officers may attach conditions, but the authority has limited capacity to inspect sites, and enforcement in comparable cases has been patchy. The report therefore recommends a financial bond, released only after restoration is complete, as the most reliable guarantee that the site returns to agriculture when working ends.
